terms.gloss: have the advantage, be better placed (in something)
terms.grammar: phrase: superior agrees with the subject; the ablative says in what
evidence: Caes. BG 7.65: quod hostēs equitātū superiōrēs esse intellegēbat
Cic. Off. 1.90: facilitāte et hūmānitāte … superiōrem fuisse
terms.comment: Latin says who is superior and in what (equitātū, in cavalry; numerō, in numbers) where English speaks of having an advantage. Lewis & Short: “of strength or success in battle or any contest, victorious, conquering, stronger, superior”.

terms.gloss: stand out, have the advantage over, be better than
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the dative of those surpassed and the ablative of the respect
evidence: Caes. BG 1.2.2: cum virtūte omnibus praestārent
Cic. Inv. 1.5: quā rē hominēs bēstiīs praestent (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Philippum quidem Macedonum rēgem rēbus gestīs et glōriā superātum ā fīliō, facilitāte et hūmānitāte videō superiōrem fuisse
phrases.english: Philip, king of Macedon, was outdone by his son in achievements and glory, but in good nature and kindness, I see, he had the advantage

phrases.latin: Caesar, quod hostēs equitātū superiōrēs esse intellegēbat …
phrases.english: Caesar, because he saw that the enemy had the advantage in cavalry …

sources: Lewis & Short: superior · Lewis & Short: praesto
Cicero, De officiis 1, and Caesar, Bellum Gallicum 1 and 7, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
